attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his core judgment and drops the 'tacit admission' framing, which is his reading of Replit's motive. It is an evaluative present-tense claim with no measure of trust or scope.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats 'can't trust... to build software' as having no threshold or task scope, so it marks the claim not adjudicable. That is fair to the words.

evidence.note: Replit's changelog confirms the autonomy-level setting was released on 2025-09-19. It is a company disclosure about the premise and says nothing about whether coding LLMs can be trusted.

reviews.rationale: The factual premise, that Replit shipped an autonomy setting, is confirmed. The claim itself is a blanket judgment about trust with no threshold, task scope or measure, and his inference about Replit's motive cannot be tested. It is too vague to score.

attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast, in the first person ('I expect').

semantics.note: 'I expect' with no qualifier is a scored forecast. 'The longer OpenAI survives' describes how long the forecast runs rather than setting a condition. No deadline is given.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: private credit means nonbank private lending, and it must be tied to OpenAI or an OpenAI project. Requiring evidence of displacement for 'sap' is reasonable. The early-resolution rule needs executed financing, not talks.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure of a $122B funding round in committed capital (2026-03-31). This fits the continued-raising part but is equity, not private credit, so it does not settle the claim.

A secondary report of early Broadcom talks to finance OpenAI's chips, with Apollo and Blackstone named as possible participants. No final terms, borrower or executed deal, so the early-resolution rule is not met.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the packet shows no executed private-credit financing for OpenAI. There is only a company-disclosed equity round and preliminary talks, so the early-resolution rule is not met. Not finding such financing yet is not failure. The forecast remains open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'Can — and will' and 'only go down' are firm, so this is a scored forecast. The revision keeps the 'five years or later' qualifier and the new-car comparison. No deadline is given.

contract.note: The lifecycle reading is ordinary and fair. It treats 'only go down' as a lifecycle trend rather than strictly monotonic prices, and 'five years or later' as no deadline. Requiring a representative cohort to resolve early is reasonable.

evidence.note: A preprint whose observation window ended in 2025. It shows a few A100 and H100 replacements but does not follow any cohort over a five-year-plus lifecycle.
NVIDIA's MLPerf post (2025-11-12) shows Blackwell outperforming Hopper. This supports only the supersession part. It is partly a company claim and mixes in software gains.

A resale index for a mixed basket of GPUs, which fell overall but rebounded to 107 in April 2026. Used H100 servers held their price. This challenges a strict 'only down' reading but does not settle the lifecycle.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the early-resolution rule (a representative cohort followed through its full lifecycle) is not met. Successor benchmarks support only one part. The resale data cover 13 months, a mixed basket and include rebounds, which do not settle lifecycle depreciation. The combined forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, in his own voice.

semantics.note: A causal claim: probabilistic nature leads to unreliable repetition. The 'because' clause and 'every single time' are both kept.

contract.note: The main reading is ordinary: repeated prompts under normal sampling. The contract also tests a stronger inherent-impossibility reading separately, which the words partly invite ('because they're probabilistic'). The result depends on which reading is applied.

evidence.note: Hugging Face's 2020 decoding guide says sampling is not deterministic. This supports the practical claim, though the guide also shows that a fixed seed reproduces output.

Thinking Machines (2025-09-10) got 1000 identical completions with batch-invariant kernels, which contradicts the inherent-impossibility reading. Its default setup varied even at temperature 0, which fits the practical claim.

reviews.rationale: The practical part holds: under ordinary sampling and default inference, identical prompts give different outputs (e1, and e2's default runs). The implication that being probabilistic makes repetition inherently impossible is contradicted: controlled inference produced identical outputs (e2). Seeded decoding (e1) points the same way.
